prompt: What are the common mistakes with interfaces in C# and how can they be avoided?
completion:
Below is a “cook‑book” style list of the *most common interface mistakes* you’ll see in real‑world C# code, why they’re problems, and concrete ways to sidestep them. It’s organized by *category* (design, naming, versioning, implementation, testing, etc.) so you can pick the items that resonate with your current project. --- ## 1. Design‑Level Mistakes | Mistake | Why It’s Bad | How to Avoid It | |---------|--------------|-----------------| | **“Fat” interfaces** – one interface that contains many unrelated members. | Violates *Interface Segregation Principle* (ISP). Clients are forced to implement or depend on methods they don’t need, making change hard. | Split into focused interfaces.
Example: `IReadable`, `IWritable`, `ISeekable` instead of one gigantic `IStream`. | | **Empty or marker interfaces** (e.g., `public interface ISerializable {}`) | Adds no contract; can be misused as a “flag” that changes behavior automatically. | Prefer attributes (`[Serializable]`) or explicit interfaces that actually expose members. | | **Using interfaces for concrete, non‑replaceable types** | Adds unnecessary abstraction and complexity. | Keep concrete classes unless you expect alternative implementations or need to inject a test double. | | **Defining interfaces that expose internal implementation details** (e.g., “IFileStream” with a `string FilePath { get; }` that leaks a path). | Tightens coupling and hides domain logic behind concrete concerns. | Expose only what the consumer needs. Keep implementation‑specific details out of the contract. | | **Changing an interface after it’s shipped** | Adds a new member or changes a signature breaks every implementation and all consumers. | Follow *Interface Versioning* rules:
• Prefer adding new interfaces instead of modifying existing ones.
• Use default interface implementations (C# 8+) to add optional members.
• Document deprecation and migration paths. | | **Using an interface to hide static helper methods** | Static methods are inherently non‑polymorphic; forcing them through an interface is unnecessary noise. | Keep helper methods in static classes or extension methods; only use interfaces for behavior that can vary. | | **Over‑splitting into many tiny interfaces that are always used together** | Increases boilerplate (multiple `new Concrete();` vs `new Concrete()`) and can make the design look fragmented. | Use a “base” interface that aggregates the others if they’re always used together; keep the others private or internal. | | **Explicit interface implementations for every member** | Makes calling code verbose (`obj.MyInterfaceMethod();`) and can hide the public API from developers. | Use explicit implementation only for members that should not appear on the public surface (e.g., `ICloneable.Clone()`). | | **Defining public interfaces for internal classes** | Exposes an API that callers should not rely on, increasing future breakage risk. | Make the interface `internal` if it’s only for DI, testing, or cross‑assembly plumbing. | --- ## 2. Naming & Convention Mistakes | Mistake | Why It’s Bad | Remedy | |---------|--------------|--------| | **Interface names that do not start with “I”** (e.g., `CustomerService`). | Breaks C# conventions; readers can’t immediately tell it’s a contract. | Always prefix interface names with “I”: `ICustomerService`. | | **Using the same name for a class and its interface** (`CustomerService` & `CustomerService`). | Confuses code readers and tools (e.g., reflection, IDE navigation). | Add the `I` prefix: `CustomerService` (class) vs `ICustomerService`. | | **Unnecessary or overly verbose names** (`IReadOnlyCollectionOfCustomerDTO`). | Makes the type hard to read and use. | Keep names concise yet expressive: `ICustomerReadOnlyCollection`. | --- ## 3. Implementation‑Level Mistakes | Mistake | Why It’s Bad | Remedy | |---------|--------------|--------| | **Implementing an interface that is never used by the client** | Wastes resources, makes the API noisy. | Only implement interfaces that the consumer will actually depend on. | | **Implementing interface members that simply forward to another object** (sometimes called the “Adapter” pattern but not needed). | Adds needless indirection; can hide bugs. | Prefer composition over delegation unless you truly need to adapt a third‑party type. | | **Using interface inheritance in a “vertical” way** (e.g., `IAdvancedReader : IReader`). | Makes the type hierarchy brittle; consumers end up with a large inheritance chain. | Prefer *composition* or *explicit interface implementation* for optional capabilities. | | **Mixing data‑structures and behavior in the same interface** (e.g., `IList` has methods for mutation and queries). | It’s okay for `IList`, but you shouldn’t add unrelated methods. | Keep data‑structure interfaces (e.g., `IList`, `IReadOnlyCollection`) separate from domain behavior. | | **Returning concrete types in interface members** (`List GetTags()` in `ITagProvider`). | Forces callers to depend on a specific collection implementation. | Return `IEnumerable` or another interface that represents the contract. | --- ## 4. Versioning & Compatibility Mistakes | Mistake | Why It’s Bad | Remedy | |---------|--------------|--------| | **Adding a method to an interface that all consumers must implement** | Breaks binary compatibility (for COM, plugin scenarios). | Add a new interface instead (`IFooV2 : IFoo`). | | **Using default interface methods (C# 8+) to add optional members without versioning** | Existing code that implements the interface before the default is added must be recompiled; otherwise the default is not used. | Always keep the original interface stable; add a new one for new functionality. | | **Removing an interface member in a minor release** | Violates binary compatibility. | Never remove members; mark them obsolete and keep them until the next major version. | --- ## 5. Testing & Dependency‑Injection Mistakes | Mistake | Why It’s Bad | Remedy | |---------|--------------|--------| | **Creating a public interface solely for the sake of mocking** | Exposes internal implementation details to the public API and couples tests to production code. | Make the interface `internal` or use *private* mocks (Moq’s `Mock.Of()` with `MockBehavior.Loose`). | | **Using interfaces for data‑transfer objects (DTOs)** | DTOs are already concrete value carriers; interfaces add indirection. | Keep DTOs as plain classes. | | **Over‑mocking: mocking every dependency, even those that are simple value objects** | Test maintenance overhead increases; mocks become brittle. | Mock only *behaviors* that are external or expensive (DB, network). Use concrete types for simple logic. | | **Relying on interfaces that cannot be implemented by a stub** (e.g., an interface that includes async methods returning `Task`). | The mock must provide async behavior; a naive stub will block or throw. | Use `async` test helpers, or provide default async stubs. | | **Injecting concrete types into constructors instead of interfaces** | Tightly couples the class to a particular implementation; harder to test. | Prefer constructor injection with `IWhatever`. | --- ## 6. Practical Tips & Patterns 1. **Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) first** *Write one interface for each distinct consumer’s needs.* ```csharp public interface IReadable { Stream OpenRead(); } public interface IWritable { Stream OpenWrite(); } ``` 2. **Use `internal` interfaces for DI plumbing** ```csharp // In the service assembly internal interface IEmailSender { void Send(string to, string body); } ``` 3. **Prefer static helpers or extension methods for pure utilities** ```csharp public static class StringExtensions { public static bool IsNullOrWhiteSpace(this string s) => string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s); } ``` 4. **Avoid “marker” interfaces** - Instead of `IEntity`, use a base class or attribute (`[Entity]`). - Instead of `IComparable`, use the generic `IComparable`. 5. **Version your interfaces** ```csharp public interface IFileReader { Stream Read(); } public interface IFileReaderV2 : IFileReader { Task ReadAsync(); } ``` 6. **Keep public interfaces small** - Aim for 3‑5 members. - If you need more, break them into smaller sub‑interfaces. 7. **Use explicit implementation sparingly** ```csharp public class MyCollection : IList, ICustomEnumerable { // Public API public string this[int index] { get => ...; set => ...; } // Hidden API string ICustomEnumerable.GetName() => "HiddenName"; } ``` 8. **Prefer `IEnumerable` over `ICollection` when only reading** - This gives callers flexibility to use any collection that can be enumerated. 9. **Avoid throwing from interface implementations in production code** - Use `ArgumentNullException` or `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` where appropriate, but don’t let an interface define the behavior. 10. **Leverage default interface implementations (C# 8+) carefully** - They’re great for optional methods, but don’t change them later; treat them like extension methods. --- ## 7. Quick Checklist - **[ ]** Does each interface have a *single responsibility*? - **[ ]** Is the interface *small* (≤ 5 members)? - **[ ]** Are all methods generic and return *interfaces* or *abstract* types? - **[ ]** Is the name descriptive and prefixed with **I**? - **[ ]** Are you exposing implementation details? - **[ ]** Is the interface `internal` when it’s only used for DI or testing? - **[ ]** Are you adding or removing members without proper versioning? - **[ ]** Do you have explicit implementations only when necessary? - **[ ]** Are you mocking only the *behavior* you need to isolate? --- ### TL;DR - **Don’t over‑abstract.** Keep interfaces small, focused, and version‑safe. - **Don’t leak internals.** Expose only what the consumer needs. - **Don’t expose every method.** Use ISP to split responsibilities. - **Name them properly.** “I” prefix, concise, descriptive. - **Version carefully.** Add new interfaces or use default methods, never break existing ones. - **Internal is your friend.** Use it for plumbing, not for public API. With these guidelines, you’ll avoid the most common interface pitfalls and build code that’s easier to test, maintain, and evolve. Happy coding!
